blocks.prompt: The Goat That Climbs
blocks.text: A baby goat is called a kid. A kid can stand up about an hour after it is born. Soon it can run and jump. Goats love to climb. Their feet are split into two toes. The outside is hard. The inside is soft and rubbery, like the bottom of a climbing shoe. That is how a goat holds on to a bumpy rock. Goats do not eat tin cans. They eat leaves and twigs. A goat has no front teeth on top. It has a hard pad there instead. It grabs a leaf with its lips and pulls.

3.title: The Goat With Rectangle Eyes
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8

blocks.prompt: Built for Climbing
blocks.text: Goats are made for going up. A goat's foot is not one solid hoof. It is split into two toes, and the goat can spread them apart to hug a narrow ledge. Around the edge of each toe is a hard rim, like the toe of a climbing shoe. Inside that rim is a soft pad that grips rough rock. A goat can stand on a ledge no wider than your hand. In the mountains of Italy there is a tall dam wall, almost straight up and down. Wild goats called ibex climb it. They pick their way across the stones, and they do it for salt. The rock face leaks minerals the goats cannot find in the grass below, so up they go. Goats also climb trees. In Morocco, goats walk out along the branches of argan trees to reach the fruit. From far away, the tree looks like it grew goats.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.
items: What are the two parts of a goat's toe, and what does each one do?
Why do the ibex in Italy climb the dam wall?
What do the goats in Morocco climb trees to reach?
Why do you think a goat can stand on a ledge that a horse could not?
answers: a hard rim around the edge and a soft pad inside that grips the rock
to reach salt and minerals leaking out of the rock face
the fruit of the argan tree
(inference: its toes spread and grip, and it is small and light)

4.title: The Goat With Rectangle Eyes
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Pupils are wide rectangles
Field of view: about 320 to 340 degrees
Eyes rotate to stay level with the ground
Horses, sheep, and deer share the trick
Cats hunt, so their pupils are vertical slits

blocks.prompt: Eyes Like Letterboxes
blocks.text: Look closely at a goat's eye. The dark pupil is not a circle or a vertical slit. It is a wide rectangle lying on its side, like a letterbox cut into the iris. This shape is not an accident. A goat is a prey animal. It spends its life eating with its head down, which is exactly when something hungry is most likely to sneak up. A letterbox pupil lets in a broad, flat band of light, so the goat sees a sharp panorama of the ground and the horizon while the sky above stays blurry. It does not need the sky. It needs to know what is moving in the grass. Together, a goat's two eyes cover somewhere between 320 and 340 degrees. It can see nearly all the way around itself without turning its head. Then comes the clever part. When a goat lowers its head to feed, the pupils do not tip with it. Each eye rotates in its socket, by as much as 50 degrees, so the rectangle stays level with the ground. Scientists at a university in California measured this in goats and other plant eaters, and found the same trick in horses, sheep, and deer. Now compare a cat. A cat is a hunter, and its pupil is a vertical slit, which helps it judge exactly how far away a mouse is before it pounces. Prey animals want width. Hunters want distance. The eye tells you the job.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: Describe the shape of a goat's pupil and explain why that shape suits a prey animal.
What happens to a goat's eyes when it lowers its head to feed, and why does that matter?
The passage says a goat does not need the sky. Explain what that means.
Why does a cat have a vertical pupil instead of a horizontal one?
answers: a wide rectangle lying on its side; it gives a broad, sharp view of the ground and horizon where danger comes from
each eye rotates up to about 50 degrees so the rectangle stays level with the ground; it keeps the wide view working while the goat eats
(inference: nothing dangerous arrives from above, so sharp sky vision is not worth having)
it hunts, and a vertical slit helps it judge distance before it pounces

blocks.prompt: Circle the main idea of this passage.

answers: A goat's rectangular pupil is built to give a prey animal a wide, level view of the ground

5.title: The Goat With Rectangle Eyes
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Capra hircus, from the wild bezoar ibex
Domesticated about 10,000 years ago
Four stomach chambers; the rumen does the work
Browsers: leaves, twigs, scrub, bark
Close to a billion goats on Earth today

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Turned Weeds Into Milk
blocks.text: About ten thousand years ago, in the rocky hills of what is now western Iran, people began keeping goats. The dog had come to us earlier, as a hunting partner. The goat was different. The goat was the first walking food supply. The wild ancestor was the bezoar ibex, a tough, horned climber of dry mountains. It was a strange choice for a farm animal, and a brilliant one. Goats are browsers, not grazers. A sheep wants a field of grass. A goat wants the things nobody else can use: thorny scrub, bitter leaves, twigs, bark, the weeds at the edge of the stony ground. Land that would starve a cow will keep a goat. What lets a goat live on that diet is a stomach with four rooms. The largest, the rumen, is a warm tank holding billions of microbes. The goat cannot digest the tough fiber in a leaf. Its microbes can. They break it down, and the goat lives on what they release. The goat brings mouthfuls back up, chews them again, and swallows them down. That is what chewing the cud means. A goat is not really eating leaves. It is farming a colony of microbes and eating the harvest. For a family on hard ground, this was everything. A goat converted worthless scrub into milk every day, and into cheese that kept. It gave hair, hide, and meat. It was small enough for one person to carry and stubborn enough to survive a journey. Goats went with people out of the Middle East, across Africa, into Europe and Asia, up mountains and onto ships. Sailors dropped them on islands so that future crews would find food waiting. That last habit shows the other side of the story. A goat that can eat anything will eat everything. Set loose on an island with no predators, goats have stripped whole landscapes bare and pushed native plants to extinction. The same appetite that fed the first farmers has ruined ecosystems that took millions of years to grow. There are close to a billion goats on Earth today. That number is a monument to a good decision, and a bill that other species keep paying.

6.title: The Goat With Rectangle Eyes
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Capra hircus, domesticated about 10,000 years ago
Kids raised together develop similar calls
Solved a puzzle box, remembered it 10 months later
Look to humans when a task is impossible
Prefer photographs of smiling faces
Bred for milk and meat, never for cooperation

blocks.prompt: What the Goat Knows
blocks.text: For most of history, the goat has been treated as a stomach with legs. It was among the first animals people farmed, roughly ten thousand years ago, and we kept it for a simple reason: it turns worthless scrub into milk. Nobody bred a goat for cleverness. Nobody needed it to understand us. That assumption went unexamined for a hundred centuries, and then, in the last twenty years, a small group of researchers decided to actually test it. Start with the voice. In 2012, biologists at Queen Mary University of London recorded goat kids raised in different social groups and compared their calls. The kids in a group sounded like each other, and less like kids from other groups. When the researchers moved animals into new groups, the calls drifted toward the new company. The word the press reached for was accents, and while that word does a lot of work, the underlying finding was real: a goat's voice is shaped by who it grows up around, not fixed at birth. That is not what a stomach with legs is supposed to do. Then the box. The same team built a puzzle: pull a lever, then lift it, and food appears. Most goats in the test worked it out inside a dozen attempts, without copying a demonstrator. Ten months later, the researchers brought them back. The goats solved it again in under a minute. Ten months is a long time to hold a piece of information you have no reason to expect will ever be useful again. The most interesting result came last. Researchers gave goats a container of food and sealed it so it could not be opened. A dog, in this situation, does something specific: it stops working and looks at the nearest human, then back at the container, as if to say, you deal with this. That behavior was long thought to be a signature of dogs, the product of thousands of years of breeding animals to cooperate with us. Goats did it too. They turned to the human. They turned more when the human was facing them than when the human's back was turned, which means the goat was not simply looking around the room. It was addressing someone. A later study found that goats, shown photographs of the same person smiling and scowling, preferred to approach the smile. None of this makes a goat a genius. It makes the goat a problem for a story we tell ourselves. The comfortable version is that dogs are special, that their attention to human faces is a gift we engineered through selective breeding for partnership. But nobody bred goats to read us. We bred them for milk, hair, and meat, and they learned to read us anyway. The likeliest explanation is that simply living alongside humans for ten thousand years is enough. Domestication itself, not the specific job, may be what tunes an animal to our faces. That conclusion costs something. It is easy to think of a farm animal as a machine that eats. It is harder once you know it is watching your expression and deciding what to make of you.

answers: (original one-sentence summary)
(calls became similar within a group and drifted when groups changed; accents is borrowed from human speech and claims more than the data shows, so the author flags it)
(the box tested learning; the container tested whether a goat would appeal to a person, which was thought to be unique to dogs; cite: That behavior was long thought to be a signature of dogs)

(that dogs are uniquely tuned to humans by breeding; cite: The comfortable version is that dogs are special, that their attention to human faces is a gift we engineered through selective breeding for partnership)
(it makes the reader responsible for how they treat an animal that watches them; earned via the facing-versus-turned-back detail and the smiling-face study)
